strengths: The paper identifies a timely and useful problem: temporally dense, structured audio-visual captioning that goes beyond short event-level dense video captions and global audio-visual summaries.
The proposed output schema is practically motivated and covers dimensions that are often ignored in video captioning, including dialogue, acoustic cues, camera state, and shot editing style.

OmniDCBench is potentially valuable: 1,122 fully human-annotated videos with long structured scene-level captions would be a useful benchmark if released with clear annotation guidelines and validation.

The paper includes a reasonable specialist baseline built on Qwen2.5-Omni, with SFT plus GRPO, and reports broad comparisons across proprietary models, open-source omni models, VideoQA transfer, and temporal grounding.
The authors include an honest limitations section noting context-window constraints and weak generalization to much longer videos.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims rely heavily on the new SodaM metric, but SodaM is not sufficiently validated. Caption quality is judged by Gemini-2.5-Flash checklist matching, yet the paper does not report correlation with human judgments, judge variance, prompt sensitivity, or failure analysis. This is especially concerning because the method is also optimized with SodaM-like rewards.

The evaluation has possible judge/model bias and circularity: Gemini is used to synthesize training data, Gemini-2.5-Flash is used for the main checklist evaluation, and Gemini-2.5-Pro is used to answer downstream QA from generated captions. The paper does not adequately disentangle true caption quality from compatibility with Gemini-style descriptions or judging.

The benchmark construction lacks important reproducibility and quality-control details. The manuscript says it recruited “approximately annotators,” omitting the number; it does not provide inter-annotator agreement, pay/qualification details, adjudication rules, scene-boundary agreement, or quantitative annotation audits.

The reported improvement over Gemini-2.5-Pro is not fully convincing. Gemini has substantially better temporal F1/mIoU, while the proposed model wins on SodaM under an LLM-judge metric whose reliability is not established. The qualitative example also contains an inconsistency: the figure text says Gemini misidentifies the driver as a woman, while the shown caption under Gemini appears to describe a woman driver in a way that is not clearly tied to the same full structured output.

The method itself is mostly an application of an existing omni backbone with synthetic Gemini-generated data and standard SFT/GRPO. The task and benchmark are more original than the modeling contribution.

Several technical details are underspecified: the length reward formula is missing, checklist decomposition into atomic elements is not described in enough detail, decoding settings are absent, and the many-to-one alignment procedure is ambiguous given the dynamic programming recurrence as written.

Ablations are too limited for the scope of the claims. There is no ablation of audio vs. visual input, schema dimensions, synthetic data source, judge choice, alignment strategy, or human-vs-synthetic training data quality. The GRPO ablation is small and does not isolate all reward terms.

The downstream VideoQA protocol is indirect and potentially fragile: using generated captions as context for Gemini-2.5-Pro may measure whether captions contain answerable clues, but it does not establish that the captioner itself has improved reasoning, and the closed-source answerer introduces another uncontrolled variable.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places. There are many typos and formatting issues, e.g. “Auiod-Visual,” “exsiting,” “donimant,” “grouding,” missing release URL in the abstract, and the incomplete annotator count. These issues reduce confidence in the care of the experimental reporting.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper promises that datasets, models, and code will be released, but the current manuscript does not provide enough detail to reproduce the data pipeline, annotation process, metric implementation, or all evaluation prompts/settings independently.

Ethical treatment is brief. The work uses movie and YouTube-derived datasets and detailed dialogue transcription, but does not discuss copyright/licensing constraints, privacy risks in videos containing people, annotator labor conditions, or safeguards against surveillance-style misuse in sufficient depth.

strengths: The paper targets a useful problem: temporally grounded, audio-visual, multi-scene captioning with richer structured outputs than standard dense video captioning.
OmniDCBench, if released as described, could be a valuable benchmark because it contains 1,122 human-annotated videos with scene-level timestamps and six caption dimensions.
The authors provide a clear high-level task definition and compare against a broad set of proprietary, open-source, and specialist baselines.
The ablations suggest that additional synthetic SFT data and the SodaM/GRPO reward improve the reported benchmark score, giving some evidence that the training recipe is not arbitrary.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not convincingly supported. The main metric SodaM relies on Gemini-based checklist judging, but the paper does not validate this judge against human preferences, report judge reliability, or quantify sensitivity to prompt/model choice. Since Gemini is also used to synthesize training data, the evaluation setup risks strong judge/data bias.

SodaM is underspecified and potentially flawed. The dynamic-programming recurrence shown only supports skip-or-one-to-one matching, while the text claims many-to-one merging; it is unclear how multiple predictions are aligned to one ground-truth scene. The checklist score also appears largely recall-based and has weak penalties for hallucinated or incorrect details beyond a length reward.

The main result is weak despite strong wording: TimeChat-Captioner improves SodaM over Gemini-2.5-Pro by only 35.0 vs. 33.7, without confidence intervals, significance testing, repeated runs, or human evaluation, while Gemini remains clearly better on temporal F1 and mIoU.

The downstream evaluation is not persuasive. For VideoQA, models generate captions that Gemini-2.5-Pro then uses to answer questions, so the reported score measures a caption-plus-Gemini pipeline rather than the model's own reasoning ability. Prompting details, fairness across baselines, and possible caption-length advantages are not adequately controlled.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a main-track claim. The abstract ends with an incomplete release URL, the paper gives no concrete repository, no detailed baseline prompts, no decoding settings, no judge implementation details beyond a prompt, and requires 32x80G GPUs. The synthetic dataset construction depends heavily on Gemini-2.5-Pro, which may be difficult or expensive to reproduce exactly.

The benchmark annotation process is insufficiently documented. The paper says it recruited 'approximately annotators,' gives no number, compensation, expertise criteria, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication protocol, or measured annotation quality. This is especially concerning because camera state, shot editing, dialogue, and acoustic cues require specialized judgment.

The qualitative evidence is confusing and internally inconsistent. Figure 4 claims the proposed model aligns with all six dimensions, but the shown model output is a short unstructured paragraph and itself says 'a woman driving,' while the surrounding text criticizes Gemini for the same kind of misidentification. This undermines confidence in the analysis.

The paper makes broad claims about 'state-of-the-art' and 'significantly enhances' omni-modal alignment, but the method is mostly a specialist fine-tune of Qwen2.5-Omni on Gemini-generated data plus an LLM-judge reward. The originality is moderate, and the evidence does not establish general improvement in audio-visual understanding.

Limitations and ethics are only partially addressed. The authors mention context length and long-video generalization, but do not seriously discuss hallucination, copyright/licensing implications of movie/YouTube clips and dialogue transcription, privacy in public videos, or the risks of releasing dense scripts that can facilitate surveillance or misinformation.

Presentation quality is below the expected level: there are frequent typos and inconsistencies ('Auiod,' 'donimant,' 'Qwen-3-Omini,' 'groundtruth'), incomplete text, future/inconsistent citations, and unclear notation. These issues materially affect interpretability rather than being merely cosmetic.

strengths: The paper introduces a useful and timely task formulation, OmniDenseCaptioning, that combines continuous temporal segmentation with structured audio-visual captions across events, background, camera, editing, dialogue, and acoustics. This is a meaningful extension beyond sparse dense video captioning and global audio-visual captioning.

The benchmark contribution is valuable: OmniDCBench contains 1,122 fully human-annotated videos with rich scene-level captions averaging about 995 words per video, and the paper provides dataset statistics and annotation interface details.

The empirical results are strong. TimeChat-Captioner-7B-GRPO substantially outperforms open-source baselines on SodaM and approaches or exceeds proprietary systems on caption quality, with clear gains from SFT, GRPO, and the SodaM caption reward.

The proposed SodaM metric addresses a real evaluation difficulty: ambiguous scene boundaries. The dynamic-programming temporal alignment plus caption checklist evaluation is well motivated for this task.

The paper includes useful reproducibility details: backbone, data sources, training sizes, learning rates, batch sizes, rollout size, reward weights, sequence length, FPS, hardware, and prompt templates are reported, and the authors state that code, data, and models will be released.
The limitations section is honest about important constraints, especially the 32K context limit and weak generalization to hour-long videos.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies heavily on LLM-based judging with Gemini-2.5-Flash, but the paper does not sufficiently validate SodaM against human judgments or analyze judge variance, bias, or robustness. This is especially important because the training data are also synthesized with Gemini-2.5-Pro.

SodaM appears recall-oriented and may reward verbose captions that cover many keypoints while insufficiently penalizing hallucinations, incorrect details, or over-segmentation after many-to-one merging. The length reward partly addresses this during training, but the evaluation metric itself needs a stronger precision/error component.

Benchmark annotation details are incomplete. The appendix says “approximately annotators” without a number, and there is no report of annotator expertise, agreement, adjudication protocol, pay/quality controls, or consistency statistics for scene boundaries and six-dimensional captions.

The downstream QA evaluation is indirect: generated captions are fed to Gemini-2.5-Pro to answer questions, so gains may reflect compatibility with the Gemini answerer or caption verbosity rather than intrinsic reasoning. The WorldSense gains are also more modest than the Daily-Omni gains.

The Charades-STA transfer experiment is encouraging but not fully isolated: all models are fine-tuned on Charades-STA, and the paper does not clearly disentangle benefits from OmniDenseCaptioning pretraining, backbone choice, or training compute.

The work is expensive to reproduce in full, requiring 32x80G GPUs and closed-source Gemini APIs for synthetic data generation and SodaM judging. The promised release helps, but closed-source dependencies remain a reproducibility concern.

Presentation is generally clear but has noticeable polish issues, including typos, awkward phrasing, an apparently blank availability URL in the abstract, and some inconsistent naming such as SodaM/Gemini judge references.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful new task, OmniDenseCaptioning, aimed at continuous scene segmentation plus six-dimensional audio-visual scripting. This is a meaningful extension beyond sparse dense video captioning, especially because it explicitly includes dialogue, acoustics, camera state, and shot editing.

The benchmark effort is substantial: OmniDCBench contains 1,122 fully human-annotated videos with long structured captions averaging about 995 words per video, and the paper describes a multi-stage annotation and checking pipeline.

The proposed SodaM metric addresses a real evaluation difficulty for this task: ambiguous scene boundaries and variable numbers of predicted scenes. The dynamic-programming alignment plus many-to-one merging is well motivated, and the appendix provides useful validation against human preferences and multiple LLM judges.

The empirical results are broad and encouraging. TimeChat-Captioner-7B improves strongly over open-source baselines on OmniDCBench, exceeds Gemini-2.5-Pro on the reported SodaM score, transfers to caption-based Daily-Omni and WorldSense QA, and improves Charades-STA temporal grounding after fine-tuning.

The training recipe is reasonably well documented, including data scale, sampling rate, sequence length, SFT/GRPO hyperparameters, reward weights, compute scale, and prompt templates for synthetic data generation and judging.
The limitations section is candid about context-window constraints and weak generalization to hour-long videos, which are important limitations for dense video scripting.
weaknesses: The evaluation metric is still a central risk. SodaM is primarily checklist-recall based and appears to reward whether ground-truth atomic facts are covered, but it does not clearly penalize hallucinated or incorrect extra content. For a dense captioning task, factual precision is as important as recall, especially because long captions can include many plausible but false details.

The benchmark annotation process lacks important reliability details. The paper says annotations are double-checked and later says it recruited approximately annotators, but does not report the number of annotators, their qualifications, payment/quality controls, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedure, or consistency statistics for temporal boundaries and six-dimensional captions.

The strongest headline claim depends heavily on an LLM-judge metric and on the authors’ own benchmark. Although the appendix reports cross-judge validation and human preference correlation, the human study is small at 122 non-tie comparisons over only five systems, and the same style of checklist evaluation is also used as a GRPO reward, raising concern that the model may be optimized toward the metric rather than generally better dense captioning.

The downstream QA evaluation is indirect: generated captions are fed to Gemini-2.5-Pro as the sole context, so improvements measure compatibility with that answerer and caption completeness only indirectly. This is useful evidence, but it is weaker than evaluating end-task models or human answerability/factuality directly.

The synthetic training data pipeline is based on Gemini-2.5-Pro, while evaluation uses Gemini-2.5-Flash as the main judge and compares against Gemini-2.5-Pro. This creates possible teacher/judge/style bias that is not fully disentangled, even though the authors include some multi-judge analysis.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete in the manuscript. The abstract states that datasets, models, and code are publicly available, but the visible manuscript leaves the URL blank. Also, details such as exact baseline prompts, decoding settings, checklist/keypoint extraction procedure, and failure handling for LLM judges are not sufficiently specified.

The ablations are somewhat limited. Table 4 supports the importance of SFT scale and SodaM reward, but there is little causal analysis of individual caption dimensions, audio versus visual inputs, backbone choice, synthetic-data quality filtering, or precision/false-positive behavior.

The ethics discussion is brief. It mentions public academic datasets, bias, misinformation, and responsible licenses, but does not deeply address copyright/privacy issues around YouTube/movie-derived clips, potential misuse for surveillance or unauthorized transcription, or bias in dialogue/acoustic/cinematic descriptions.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and timely problem: temporally grounded, audio-visual dense video captioning with structured scene-level outputs. The six-dimensional schema is intuitive and could be valuable for downstream video understanding and data generation if released and validated well.

OmniDCBench is potentially a useful benchmark: it contains 1,122 fully human-annotated videos with long, structured captions, explicit scene timestamps, and coverage of events, background, camera state, shot editing, dialogue, and acoustics.

The proposed SodaM metric addresses a real evaluation issue in dense captioning: scene boundary ambiguity and variable numbers of predicted segments. The DP alignment/merging idea is reasonable, and the appendix includes useful sanity checks across several LLM judges and a small human preference study.

The empirical package is fairly broad: comparisons include proprietary and open-source omni-modal models, ablations over SFT scale and GRPO/SodaM reward, downstream caption-based VideoQA, temporal grounding on Charades-STA, and a synthetic-caption-as-training-data experiment.
weaknesses: The central performance claims depend heavily on SodaM, but SodaM is also used as the GRPO reward. This creates a strong risk of metric overfitting: the reported improvement from SFT to GRPO is exactly on the optimized LLM-judge metric, while temporal F1/mIoU slightly decrease. The paper does not provide enough independent human evaluation of the final system to establish that the claimed gains reflect real caption quality rather than reward/metric alignment.

The LLM-as-judge evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for the main claim that the model surpasses Gemini-2.5-Pro. The human validation uses only 129 pairwise comparisons over five systems, and system-level Pearson correlations are computed with N=5. This is supportive but too small to validate a new benchmark metric as the decisive basis for state-of-the-art claims.

The downstream VideoQA evaluation is only a proxy: generated captions are fed to Gemini-2.5-Pro as the answerer. This conflates caption quality with Gemini's reasoning and interpretation of each caption style, and does not show that the proposed model itself improves end-to-end audio-visual reasoning. The strongest result, Daily-Omni 52.8, still trails Gemini captions at 60.2, so the wording around downstream capability is stronger than the evidence supports.

The training data is generated by Gemini-2.5-Pro, and the model is then claimed to surpass Gemini-2.5-Pro on a Gemini-judged or LLM-judged metric. This teacher-student setup is not inherently invalid, but the paper needs stronger controls to rule out artifacts of the synthetic pipeline, annotation schema, and judge preferences.

Reproducibility is weak in the submitted manuscript. The abstract says all datasets, models, and code are publicly available, but the URL is blank. Reproducing the work also requires closed-source Gemini-2.5-Pro for training data construction, Gemini-2.5-Flash or other proprietary judges for evaluation, and 32x80G GPU training, with limited details on sampling, decoding, filtering thresholds, and exact prompts for all inference baselines.

Dataset and ethics details are incomplete. The benchmark section says OmniDCBench uses Movie101 and YT-Temporal-1B, while the impact statement says training and evaluation data are from MMTrail and Movie101. Human annotation details are also under-specified, including a missing annotator count, compensation/qualification information, inter-annotator agreement, and treatment of potentially copyrighted movie/YouTube content.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for a main-track paper. There are many typographical and grammatical issues, incomplete text, inconsistent terminology, malformed equations/tables, and some overclaiming. These problems make it harder to assess the technical contribution reliably.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and useful task, OmniDenseCaptioning, that is clearly distinguished from standard dense video captioning by requiring continuous timestamps plus rich audio-visual, dialogue, camera, and editing descriptions. This framing is significant because such script-like supervision could plausibly benefit both video understanding and generation.

The resource contribution is strong: OmniDCBench contains 1,122 fully human-annotated videos with dense multi-dimensional descriptions, and TimeChatCap-42K provides a large training set. The benchmark statistics, annotation schema, and prompts make the task concrete and relatively easy for others to understand.

The proposed SodaM metric is thoughtfully motivated for this setting. The paper recognizes the ambiguity of scene boundaries and provides DP-based temporal alignment, checklist-style semantic scoring, and useful validation against human preferences and multiple LLM judges.

The experimental results are broad and convincing overall. TimeChat-Captioner substantially improves over open-source baselines on OmniDCBench, is competitive with or above Gemini-2.5-Pro on SodaM, transfers well to caption-based omni-video QA, and improves temporal grounding on Charades-STA after fine-tuning.

The ablations support the main engineering choices: scaling SFT data helps, GRPO with SodaM improves the primary metric and downstream QA, and the DP merging analysis provides evidence that the metric better matches human judgments than stricter one-to-one matching.

Presentation is generally clear, with helpful figures, qualitative examples, implementation details, prompts, and an explicit limitations section. The authors also discuss data sources, potential misuse, and release intentions.
weaknesses: The evaluation depends heavily on LLM judges and checklist recall. Although the multi-judge and human-alignment studies are valuable, SodaM may still under-penalize hallucinated or extraneous details because it primarily checks whether ground-truth keypoints are covered. This is important for a task where long captions can contain plausible but false information.

There is some circularity or coupling in the ecosystem of data generation, evaluation, and downstream assessment: Gemini-2.5-Pro is used to synthesize training captions, Gemini-family models are involved in SodaM and QA evaluation, and Gemini-2.5-Pro is also a major comparison point. The paper mitigates this with alternate judges, but the concern is not fully eliminated.

The benchmark and training distribution are mostly short clips, with many videos around one minute and limitations acknowledged for hour-long content. This narrows the demonstrated scope despite claims about general omni-video understanding and dense supervision for long or multi-scene videos.

The downstream VideoQA protocol measures the usefulness of generated captions when passed to Gemini-2.5-Pro, rather than direct end-task performance of the captioner or downstream models. This is a reasonable proxy, but it confounds caption quality with the answerer's robustness to caption style and omissions.

Annotation and reproducibility details are helpful but incomplete in places. The appendix says approximately annotators were recruited but appears to omit the number, does not report inter-annotator agreement, and gives limited detail on annotator qualifications, compensation, or disagreement resolution beyond additional review.

The method itself is mostly an integration of existing components: Qwen2.5-Omni, synthetic Gemini data, SFT, GRPO, and LLM-based checklist evaluation. The originality lies more in task/benchmark/metric design than in model architecture or learning algorithm. That is still valuable, but it tempers the contribution relative to a strong accept.
The compute requirement is high, with training on 32x80G GPUs and long 32K-token sequences, which may limit reproducibility for many groups even if the code and data are released.
